questions.question: What does MASFT stand for and what does it catalog?
options: Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy — 14 failure modes in 3 categories
Model Accuracy and Safety Fault Testing — 10 test scenarios
Machine Agent System Failure Tracking — real-time monitoring framework
Multi-Agent Safety Framework for Testing — evaluation benchmark
questions.explanation: MASFT (Berkeley, arXiv:2503.13657) stands for Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy. It catalogs 14 failure modes clustered into 3 categories with inter-annotator Cohen's Kappa 0.88 — the categories are reliably distinguishable.

questions.question: What are the five industry-recurring agentic failure modes identified across field analyses?
options: Slow execution, wrong answers, crashes, cost overruns, poor UX
Hallucinated actions, scope creep, cascading errors, context loss, tool misuse
Prompt injection, data leakage, infinite loops, memory overflow, tool timeouts
Model drift, retrieval failure, planning errors, execution bugs, evaluation gaps
questions.explanation: Arize, Galileo, and NimbleBrain field analyses (2024-2026) converge on five recurring modes: hallucinated actions, scope creep (doing more than asked), cascading errors, context loss (forgetting early constraints), and tool misuse.

questions.question: What is 'success hallucination' and why is cascading the 'killer' failure mode?
options: Success hallucination is the model claiming to succeed when no API was called; cascading kills because it generates excessive logs

Success hallucination is the agent claiming done on a 400 error; cascading is the killer because agents cannot distinguish 'I failed' from 'impossible' and one wrong call can trigger a multi-system incident
Success hallucination means the model misunderstands the task; cascading occurs when multiple agents work simultaneously
Success hallucination is a CRITIC evaluation failure; cascading means the loop runs indefinitely
questions.explanation: Success hallucination: the agent returns success when the target state is unchanged (claims success on a 400 error). Cascading is the killer: one phantom SKU hallucination can trigger four downstream API calls resulting in a multi-system incident, because agents cannot reliably distinguish failure from 'task is impossible'.

questions.question: What is the 'instruction-following deviation' hallucination type from the LLM Agent Hallucinations Survey?
options: The agent follows instructions too literally
The agent does not follow the system prompt or user constraint
The agent produces output that is too long
The agent calls tools in the wrong order
questions.explanation: The LLM Agent Hallucinations Survey (arXiv:2509.18970) identifies two primary manifestations: Instruction-following Deviation (agent ignores system prompt or user constraint) and Long-range Contextual Misuse (agent forgets or misapplies context from earlier turns).

questions.question: What is the core claim of MASFT about agentic failures?
options: Failures will be solved by better base models
Failures are fundamental design flaws in multi-agent systems, not LLM limitations to be fixed with better models
Failures are caused by insufficient training data
Failures are primarily infrastructure problems
questions.explanation: MASFT's central claim: the identified failure modes are fundamental design flaws in multi-agent systems, not limitations of the base LLMs. Better models alone will not eliminate them — the design patterns must change.

questions.question: What mitigation approach does the lesson recommend for catching success hallucination?
options: Trust the agent's self-reported status
Re-probe actual state after the agent claims success (was the file actually created, did the database record exist)
Run a second model to review the output
Add more detailed prompting about what success means
questions.explanation: To detect success hallucination, re-probe the actual environment state after the agent claims success. Ask: is the file there? Did the API call succeed? Was the database record created? The CRITIC pattern (Lesson 05) grounds verification in external tool results.
